method.summary: This analysis compares what Boeing says about its competitive advantage in company-authored narrative text (its corporate "About Boeing" page, the Independent Board Chair's letter, and the CEO/Compensation Committee's "To Our Shareholders" letter in the proxy) against what its governance and compensation decisions, as disclosed in the same proxy statement's compensation tables, committee activity logs, and required SEC disclosures, actually reward and fund. Every element is tied to at least one citation with document, section, and page — or is marked as unnumbered front matter where the source itself does not paginate that content.
inclusionRules: A claim is treated as stated evidence when its primary purpose is persuasive or identity-defining — describing who the company says it is, what it prioritizes, or what it is capable of — even when it cites a real number as supporting color (e.g., a shareholder letter citing delivery counts).

A claim is treated as revealed evidence when its primary purpose is factual or compliance disclosure — a required table, a committee's logged activity, an incentive-plan mechanic, or a financial reconciliation — regardless of which section of the filing it appears in.
Where the same underlying fact appears in both a persuasive passage and a compliance disclosure, the compliance disclosure is cited for the revealed pyramid.
A claim is excluded if it appears only as aspirational language with no accompanying figure, mechanism, or committee action to check it against.
method.timeWindow: Fiscal year 2025, as disclosed in the 2026 DEF 14A (proxy statement) filed for the April 17, 2026 annual meeting; a small number of multi-year figures (2023–2025 long-term incentive vesting, FY2024 free cash flow) are drawn from tables in the same filing.
limitations: Only the corporate website and the 2026 proxy statement were used; the 10-K, earnings call transcripts, and independent news coverage of the 2024 737-9 door-plug accident and its aftermath were not yet incorporated, so several potentially important gaps around that history are likely understated here.

The proxy statement is itself an audience-facing, heavily reviewed document, so "revealed" here means revealed by a disclosed mechanism or figure the company was legally required to report — not revealed by private or leaked information.

Page numbers for the Independent Board Chair's letter are marked "front matter (unnumbered)" because the source document itself does not paginate that section; a couple of other page citations are given as a range where the underlying content spans a page break.
One fiscal year of individual-performance-score data is a thin base for judging whether the flat 100% pattern (see R-B3) is a one-time transition decision or a recurring practice.

elements.claim: Core values: safety, quality, and integrity
elements.detail: Boeing's corporate "About Boeing" page names safety, quality, and integrity as its core values and frames its culture as being built on them, positioning these as foundational rather than incidental.

evidence.section: About Boeing
evidence.excerpt: Boeing is committed to fostering a culture based on our core values of safety, quality and integrity.

elements.claim: Long-standing tradition of aerospace leadership and innovation
elements.detail: The company frames continuous product-line innovation as an inherited priority ("long tradition") rather than a new initiative, and ties it explicitly to meeting emerging customer needs.

evidence.section: About Boeing
evidence.excerpt: Boeing has a long tradition of aerospace leadership and innovation. The company continues to expand its product line and services to meet emerging customer needs.

elements.claim: 182,000+ person global workforce plus an extended supplier talent base
elements.detail: Boeing frames the scale and geographic reach of its own employees, together with the skilled workforce of its supplier base, as a resource underpinning operations across more than 65 countries.

evidence.section: About Boeing
evidence.excerpt: Boeing employs more than 182,000 people across the United States and in more than 65 countries... Our enterprise also leverages the talents of hundreds of thousands more skilled people working for Boeing suppliers worldwide.

elements.metric: 182,000+ direct employees across 65+ countries, plus "hundreds of thousands" of supplier-employed workers (company-stated, undated headcount claim)

elements.claim: Integrated design, engineering, and financing capability across commercial, defense, and technology products
elements.detail: Boeing describes one coherent capability set spanning commercial airplane development, military platform design/integration, advanced technology solutions, and customer financing/service arrangements, rather than presenting these as separate, unrelated businesses.

evidence.section: About Boeing
evidence.excerpt: Its broad range of capabilities includes creating new, more efficient members of its commercial airplane family; designing, building and integrating military platforms and defense systems; creating advanced technology solutions; and arranging innovative financing and service options for customers.

elements.claim: Executes through three integrated business units serving 150+ countries
elements.detail: The stated operating structure — Commercial Airplanes; Defense, Space & Security; and Global Services — is presented as how the company turns its capabilities into products and services delivered to customers worldwide.

evidence.section: About Boeing
evidence.excerpt: Boeing is organized into three business units: Commercial Airplanes; Defense, Space & Security; and Global Services.

elements.claim: Record 2025 output: 600 deliveries (most since 2018) and ~$680B backlog across all three business units
elements.detail: Boeing's shareholder-facing letters cite 2025 operating results — the highest commercial delivery count since 2018, winning the F-47 fighter contract, and a record ~$680 billion backlog — as the concrete proof point for its narrative of successful stabilization and continued industry leadership.

evidence.section: Message from Our Independent Board Chair
evidence.excerpt: Delivering 600 commercial aircraft, the highest number since 2018... Winning the F-47 contract to design, build and deliver the U.S. Air Force's next generation fighter aircraft... Growing total company backlog to approximately $680 billion as of year-end, reflecting the strength of our portfolio, long-term resilience of our business and customer confidence in the progress we have made.

evidence.section: Approve, on an Advisory Basis, Named Executive Officer Compensation (Item 2) — To Our Shareholders
evidence.excerpt: increasing commercial airplane deliveries by 72% compared to 2024, lower cash usage and generation of positive free cash flow in the second half of the year for the first time since 2023, and increased demand for our products and services as reflected in record-breaking backlogs across all three business units and a total company backlog of approximately $680 billion as of 2025 year-end.

elements.metric: 600 commercial deliveries FY2025 (+72% vs FY2024, per company letter); ~$680B total company backlog at 2025 year-end (per company letter)

elements.claim: Rigorous "pay for performance": no payouts if performance thresholds aren't met
elements.detail: Boeing states as a core compensation principle that incentive pay is strictly contingent on achieving performance, listing "no performance-based incentive payouts if performance levels are not achieved" as a governance commitment, and frames its own ability to adjust incentive metrics as limited to what "more accurately reflect[s] the core operating performance of the company."

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Executive Summary, How We Align Pay to Shareholder Interests
evidence.excerpt: No performance-based incentive payouts if performance levels are not achieved

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — 2025 Executive Compensation Structure, Annual Incentive Plan
evidence.excerpt: The Compensation Committee limits its ability to adjust reported financial results for incentive plan purposes to circumstances where such adjustments are necessary to more accurately reflect the core operating performance of the company, pursuant to criteria approved at the time of goal-setting.

elements.claim: Balance-sheet repair and credit-rating protection outrank shareholder cash returns
elements.detail: The company has not paid a dividend since March 2020, and 2025 Finance Committee oversight focused on liquidity stress-testing, credit-rating engagement, and divesting a business line specifically to strengthen the balance sheet — while free cash flow remained negative across both disclosed fiscal years.

evidence.section: Compensation of Directors — Retainer Stock Units
evidence.excerpt: Our company has not issued a dividend since March 2020.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Board Committees, Finance Committee Key Focus Areas and Activities in 2025
evidence.excerpt: Reviewed Boeing's financial condition, including liquidity under various stress case scenarios, debt maturity profiles, repayment plans, long-range investment plan and financial exposures... Oversaw management's continued proactive engagement with credit rating agencies and investors... Oversaw the sale of portions of Boeing's digital aviation solutions business as part of our strategy to focus on core businesses, strengthen our balance sheet and prioritize our investment grade credit rating.

evidence.section: Appendix A: Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures
evidence.excerpt: Operating cash flow (GAAP) $1,065 [million, FY2025]... Less additions to property, plant & equipment ($2,942)... Free cash flow (non-GAAP) ($1,877) [million]. [FY2024: operating cash flow ($12,080); less capex ($2,230); free cash flow ($14,310).]

elements.metric: Free cash flow: –$1.877B (FY2025), –$14.31B (FY2024); no dividend since March 2020; no share buybacks disclosed in this filing

elements.claim: Pay is overwhelmingly tied to one company-wide financial/operational score, and outcomes track it closely
elements.detail: Beginning with the 2025 annual incentive plan, Boeing introduced a single enterprise-wide metric (the "One Company Score") governing payouts for the executive team and much of the global workforce. 2025 outcomes moved with it in both directions: the annual incentive paid out well above target, while a prior long-term grant paid out well below target after missing a free-cash-flow gate.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Annual Incentive Plan, One Company Score
evidence.excerpt: For 2025, we shifted to a single enterprise-wide incentive score based 80% on performance against pre-established financial targets for free cash flow, core earnings/(loss) per share and revenue, and 20% on progress toward achieving specific operational safety and execution priorities. This One Company Score determines payouts not only for our executive officers, but for our entire executive team and over 100,000 of our employees around the world, and serves to unify our workforce around our common mission.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Annual Incentive Plan, Safety & Execution Operational Scorecard
evidence.excerpt: The financial and operational performance described above resulted in a One Company Score of 131% for our 2025 annual incentive plan.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Long-Term Incentive Program
evidence.excerpt: Messrs. Gerry and West and Ms. Pope received long-term incentive awards for the 2023-2025 performance period in the form of PSUs weighted at 55% of target... the PSUs, which were based on three-year cumulative free cash flow performance against pre-set goals, paid out at 0%.

elements.metric: 93% of 2025 CEO target pay was variable; 2025 annual incentive paid at 131% of target; 2023–2025 long-term incentive realized at 51% of target (0% for the 2023 PSU tranche) after missing a free-cash-flow threshold

elements.claim: Individual behavior scores were kept flat at 100% for every named executive in 2025
elements.detail: Although the compensation program includes an individual performance multiplier explicitly meant to reward or penalize how executives embody the company's Values and Behaviors (including safety and quality), the Compensation Committee scored every NEO at exactly 100% in 2025 — the neutral target — producing no upward or downward adjustment for any executive, explicitly to reinforce a "one-team approach" rather than to differentiate individual behavior.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Annual Incentive Plan, Individual Performance Score
evidence.excerpt: For 2025, the Compensation Committee (and the Board, with respect to Mr. Ortberg) approved individual performance scores at target for all our NEOs, resulting in no adjustment to any NEO's annual incentive payout.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Annual Incentive Plan, Individual Performance Score
evidence.excerpt: Recognition of the teamwork and collaboration among members of our senior leadership team and across all areas of the businesses and functions they lead, which contributed to significantly improved financial and operational performance during 2025; and Reinforcement of the one-team approach adopted by our annual incentive plan structure in 2025, to drive alignment on operational priorities, accountability and a culture of unity.

elements.metric: 0 of 6 NEOs received an individual performance score above or below the 100% target in 2025 (multiplier range is 0%–120%)

elements.claim: Reacquired in-house fuselage/structures manufacturing via the Spirit AeroSystems acquisition
elements.detail: Completed the acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems in 2025, bringing previously outsourced 737 fuselage and other structural manufacturing back in-house, explicitly framed by the Finance Committee as strengthening production and supply-chain stability; defect rates at the acquired operation are already reported as improved.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Board Committees, Finance Committee Key Focus Areas and Activities in 2025
evidence.excerpt: Oversaw the completion of the acquisition of Spirit AeroSystems, including the status of regulatory approvals, the expected financial impact of the acquisition, the paydown of certain Spirit debt in connection with closing and the integration strategy.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Key Areas of Board Oversight, Safety and Quality, Eliminating Defects
evidence.excerpt: Reduced defects in 737 fuselage assembly at Spirit AeroSystems by an average of 45% since March 2024, through increasing inspection points at build locations and implementing customer quality approval process.

elements.metric: 737 fuselage defect rate down ~45% at Spirit AeroSystems since March 2024 (per company disclosure); acquisition completed 2025

elements.claim: FAA-aligned six-KPI production health system that gates rate increases
elements.detail: Boeing operates a formal, six-KPI framework (employee proficiency, notice-of-escape rework hours, supplier shortages, rework hours per airplane, travelers at factory rollout, and ticketing performance), developed with the FAA, to assess production-system health and determine readiness for rate increases — a repeatable, documented capability rather than an ad hoc judgment call.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Key Areas of Board Oversight, Safety and Quality
evidence.excerpt: The plan also sets forth measures to continuously monitor and manage the health of our production system through six key performance indicators (KPIs) focused on safety and production health: employee proficiency, notice of escape rework hours, supplier shortages, rework hours per airplane, travelers at factory rollout and ticketing performance. Each KPI has defined criteria that help identify areas of potential risk to our operations and trigger risk monitoring and corrective action through our SMS.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Annual Incentive Plan, Safety & Execution Operational Scorecard
evidence.excerpt: These KPIs provide a real-time mechanism for assessing the health of our production system and determining readiness for production rate increases.

elements.metric: 6 defined KPIs gate all production rate increases (per company disclosure)

elements.claim: Divested part of the digital aviation solutions business to fund balance-sheet repair
elements.detail: Rather than expanding technology/services offerings, Boeing sold portions of its digital aviation solutions business during 2025, explicitly to concentrate on core businesses, strengthen the balance sheet, and protect its investment-grade credit rating — a real portfolio-narrowing action, not a growth move.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Board Committees, Finance Committee Key Focus Areas and Activities in 2025
evidence.excerpt: Oversaw the sale of portions of Boeing's digital aviation solutions business as part of our strategy to focus on core businesses, strengthen our balance sheet and prioritize our investment grade credit rating.

evidence.section: Ratify the Appointment of Independent Auditor (Item 3) — Independent Auditor Fees
evidence.excerpt: Fees in 2025 primarily relate to professional services rendered for the audits of carve-out financial statements required in connection with the sale of portions of Boeing Global Services segment's digital aviation solutions business. These fees have been reimbursed to us by the buyer.

elements.metric: Divestiture required carve-out audit fees of $4.5M in 2025 (Audit-Related Fees), reimbursed by the buyer

elements.claim: New CEO-driven culture program: formal behavior scoring, board-level oversight, and public safety/quality reporting
elements.detail: Under CEO Kelly Ortberg, Boeing has stood up a formal "Values and Behaviors" performance-management system that scores how work gets done (not just what gets accomplished), added recurring board-level culture briefings and frequent CEO-led engagement at all levels, and committed to publicly disclosing safety and quality progress on a dedicated website.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Human Capital Management, Culture
evidence.excerpt: In February 2025, we ran more than 100 focus groups and offered an all-employee culture survey (in which 82% of our workforce participated) to gather perspectives on engagement, senior leadership effectiveness, manager effectiveness, belonging, ways of working, culture and values... In April 2025, we released our new Values and Behaviors to make our expectations clear to all of our Boeing employees. These Values and Behaviors are incorporated into our leadership development programs and are fundamental elements of our performance management system.

evidence.section: Corporate Governance — Human Capital Management, Culture
evidence.excerpt: This new process features goal setting and feedback sessions, incorporating elements of "what" employees accomplish (goals) and "how" they achieve those goals (Values and Behaviors) in determining how we reward and incentivize performance. For employees who receive individual performance scores (which act as a multiplier for annual incentive payouts), the "how" is assigned a heavier weighting in the scoring than the "what," to incentivize employees to exemplify our Values and Behaviors.

elements.claim: Switched executive long-term pay to premium-priced stock options in 2025 because leadership couldn't set reliable 3-year targets
elements.detail: For the 2025-2027 cycle, Boeing removed performance stock units (which require pre-set 3-year financial targets) from executive long-term pay entirely, replacing them with premium-priced stock options, explicitly because business volatility made it impossible to set realistic long-range goals — reversing course again in early 2026 once results stabilized enough to reintroduce targets.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Long-Term Incentive Program
evidence.excerpt: The Compensation Committee determined that an adjustment to the mix of vehicles used to deliver long-term incentives (from PSUs to PPSOs) was necessary due to the uncertainty of our business environment, primarily caused by operational challenges, regulatory and geopolitical volatility, lingering impacts of the IAM work stoppage and supply chain disruption.

evidence.section: Compensation Discussion and Analysis — Early 2026 Changes to Our Program
evidence.excerpt: While PPSOs were determined to be the most appropriate vehicle in 2025 given the challenges to long-range goal setting caused by our volatile business environment, our progress toward stabilization last year enabled the Compensation Committee to shift to incorporating an award component linked to pre-set target performance levels this year.

elements.metric: 0% of the 2025 LTI mix used pre-set 3-year PSU targets (55% PPSO/45% RSU); 2026 LTI mix reintroduced PSUs at 30% of target

gaps.title: Rigorous "pay for performance" claim vs. a metric adjustment that helped produce a 131% payout amid negative cash flow
gaps.whatDiffers: Boeing states it limits incentive-metric adjustments to what "more accurately reflect[s] the core operating performance of the company" and lists "no performance-based incentive payouts if performance levels are not achieved" as a governance commitment. In practice, for the 2025 annual incentive, free cash flow was adjusted upward from a reported ($1.9B) to ($0.5B) — alongside upward adjustments to revenue and a downward adjustment to core EPS — to reflect the Spirit AeroSystems acquisition and the digital-aviation divestiture, helping produce a 131% One Company Score payout in a year the company's own non-GAAP reconciliation still shows free cash flow at ($1.877B) and no dividend has been paid since 2020. By contrast, the Committee made no adjustments to the 2023-2025 PSU metric, which paid out at 0%.
gaps.strategicMeaning: The stated discipline ("adjust only to reflect core performance," "no payout without real performance") held in one direction — the unadjusted PSU metric paid zero — but the same discipline permitted a favorable adjustment on the metric funding the much larger annual bonus pool for over 100,000 employees. This doesn't prove the pay-for-performance claim is false: both adjustments are disclosed and tied to specific, named transactions. But it shows the "rigor" is exercised with real discretion, and in 2025 that discretion moved toward a bigger payout in the plan that pays the most people.
gaps.classificationReasoning: Not a clean misalignment: both the adjustment and the non-adjustment are disclosed, transaction-linked, and reviewed by the Compensation Committee, so nothing is hidden. It also isn't obviously deliberate positioning for an external audience, since the reconciliation detail sits in a footnote-style appendix most readers would skip. Resolving this would require knowing whether the same transaction-based adjustment logic was even available to the PSU calculation and was deliberately withheld, or whether the PSU program's own rules simply don't permit that category of adjustment.

gaps.title: Values-and-Behaviors pay link claimed vs. a mechanism that produced zero individual differentiation in its first year
gaps.whatDiffers: Boeing states that its performance-management system "measures how an employee does their work, in addition to what they accomplish," with the "how" (Values and Behaviors, including safety and quality) explicitly weighted heavier than the "what" in individual scoring. In its first year of operation, the individual performance multiplier — the only lever that turns individual behavior into individual pay — was set to exactly 100% (the neutral midpoint of a 0%–120% range) for all six named executives, with the stated rationale being team unity rather than an assessment that every executive behaved identically well.
gaps.strategicMeaning: A mechanism can exist and even be well designed on paper without yet being used to differentiate pay. Year one of the individual score gives no evidence either way about whether the "how" will ever move an executive's pay up or down in practice — it could become a real lever in future years, or it could remain a formality that defaults to target. This is worth tracking in next year's proxy rather than concluding either way now.
gaps.classificationReasoning: Genuinely unclear rather than misalignment: the company explicitly disclosed and explained the decision to score everyone at 100%, which is transparent, not hidden, and may reflect a legitimate first-year choice to build trust in a new system before penalizing anyone. It would become a stronger misalignment finding only if the same flat 100% pattern repeats in future years despite the company continuing to claim behavior-based differentiation.

gaps.title: Confident "long tradition of innovation" narrative vs. an admission the business was too unpredictable to set 3-year pay targets
gaps.whatDiffers: Boeing's public self-description claims a "long tradition of aerospace leadership and innovation" and continuous expansion to meet emerging customer needs. Internally, for the entire 2025 long-term incentive cycle, the Compensation Committee removed pre-set 3-year performance targets from executive pay altogether — replacing them with premium-priced stock options — explicitly because "the uncertainty of our business environment" made realistic long-range goal-setting impossible, alongside continued negative free cash flow and no dividend since 2020.
gaps.strategicMeaning: A company confident in sustained innovation-led growth would be expected to set, and stand behind, multi-year financial targets for the people most responsible for hitting them. For one full cycle, Boeing's own compensation committee judged its outlook too unpredictable to do that, only restoring targets once 2025 showed enough stabilization. The "tradition of leadership and innovation" framing describes an identity; the 2025 pay decision describes an actual, temporary admission of limited forward visibility.
gaps.classificationReasoning: This leans toward misalignment rather than mere positioning because the PPSO decision wasn't a marketing choice — it was an internal governance response to genuine forecasting difficulty that sits in real tension with a narrative of confident, steady innovation-led growth. It is a defensible, transparently disclosed decision, and one the company itself reversed within a year, which is why it stops short of a severe or intentional misrepresentation — but the two statements describe different realities for the same period.

trackAnalysis: On the large-public track, Boeing's 2026 DEF 14A turned out to be the richest single source for revealed evidence, because nearly every claim about priorities can be checked against a dollar figure, a committee action, or a required disclosure table in the same document. The clearest finding is that Boeing's revealed pyramid right now describes a company in stabilization mode rather than growth mode: no dividend since March 2020, negative free cash flow in both disclosed fiscal years, an admitted inability to set reliable 3-year executive targets for the entire 2025 cycle, and Finance Committee attention centered on credit-rating protection and a business divestiture rather than expansion. This sits alongside a stated identity built on a "long tradition of aerospace leadership and innovation" — a tension best read as the company using confident identity language to hold a narrative together while its own pay decisions concede, in the same document, that near-term visibility was still too limited to bet executive pay on. A second, track-specific finding is that safety commands real disclosure weight (a dedicated Aerospace Safety Committee, a named Chief Aerospace Safety Officer, safety KPIs woven into the incentive design) but a comparatively modest formal weight inside the pay formula itself (20% of the One Company Score, versus 80% financial), and the one mechanism built to reward individual safety/quality behavior — the individual performance multiplier — was not used to differentiate a single named executive in its first year. None of this is hidden: Boeing discloses all of it in the same filing, which is exactly why most of these findings are classified "unclear" rather than "misalignment" — the proxy is transparent about the tension even where it doesn't resolve it. Where the record does support a firmer "misalignment" call (G3), it is because an internal governance decision (removing performance targets from pay) sits in direct, dated tension with a public identity claim, not because anything was concealed. As an aside not built into a full gap card: the same document also shows Boeing citing record 2025 deliveries and backlog (S-T2) as proof of momentum in the same year it was divesting a technology business line (R-T1) — a smaller version of the same stabilization-over-expansion pattern.
